title: Classroom Size & STEM Graduation Rates
raw_claim: Reducing elementary classroom sizes below 15 students directly increases long-term high school STEM graduation rates by 35% across all socioeconomic demographics.

sub_claims.text: Classroom size reduction below 15 students improves 4th-grade math & science assessment scores.
sub_claims.original_claim_segment: Reducing elementary classroom sizes below 15 students improves early STEM scores
sub_claims.boundary_gap_description: Well-supported by STAR project RCT data for primary grades 1-4.

sub_claims.text: Early academic improvements directly translate into 35% higher high school STEM graduation rates.
sub_claims.original_claim_segment: directly increases long-term high school STEM graduation rates by 35%
sub_claims.boundary_gap_description: UNSUPPORTED BOUNDARY GAP: Longitudinal tracking stops at Grade 8. No statistical evidence supports a 35% gain at high school graduation.

sub_claims.text: The intervention effect is uniform across all socioeconomic demographics.
sub_claims.boundary_gap_description: UNSUPPORTED BOUNDARY GAP: Evidence shows benefits are heavily concentrated in Title I underfunded schools with high student-teacher ratios.

evidence.source_title: Project STAR: Longitudinal Effects of Small Class Sizes in Early Grades
evidence.authors: Krueger, A. B., & Whitmore, D. W.
evidence.quote_snippet: Students randomly assigned to small classes (13-17 pupils) in K-3 scored 0.20 to 0.28 standard deviations higher on standardized reading and math tests.

evidence.source_title: Middle School Retention and STEM Track Selection in Tennessee Cohorts
evidence.authors: Nye, B., Hedges, L. V., & Konstantopoulos, S.
evidence.quote_snippet: Class size benefits persist through Grade 8 math enrollment, showing a modest 4.2% increase in advanced algebra placement. Long-term graduation tracking was unavailable.

evidence.source_title: Heterogeneous Effects of Class-Size Reduction Policies
evidence.authors: Dynarski, S., Hyman, J., & Schanzenbach, D. W.
evidence.quote_snippet: Small class effects on college enrollment were statistically significant only for minority and economically disadvantaged students, with near-zero impact on affluent suburban peers.

ebdf_deltas.delta_scope: Evidence tested primary grade (K-3) classrooms in a single state; Claim scope generalizes to all elementary grades nationwide.
ebdf_deltas.delta_certainty: Evidence establishes modest 4.2% middle-school algebra bump; Claim asserts 35% definitive causal boost in STEM graduation.
ebdf_deltas.delta_temporal: Evidence longitudinal tracking ends at Grade 8 (age 14); Claim extrapolates 8 years into high school graduation.
ebdf_deltas.delta_causal: Claim omits key confounding factors: high school teacher turnover, curriculum availability, and peer group influence.

stress_test_results.attack_hypothesis: Test if 35% STEM graduation bump holds in high-income suburban school districts.
stress_test_results.attacked_condition: Suburban affluent districts with existing low baseline ratios (1:18).
stress_test_results.breaking_point_explanation: FAILED: Effect size collapses to near-zero (+0.8% statistically insignificant) when baseline resources are already high.

stress_test_results.attack_hypothesis: Test if K-3 class size advantage persists through high school without middle school interventions.
stress_test_results.attacked_condition: Grade 9-12 high school transition without continued class size capping.
stress_test_results.breaking_point_explanation: FAILED: Academic fade-out dynamics attenuate over 5+ years, requiring ongoing intervention to sustain gains.

stress_test_results.attack_hypothesis: Test whether class size reduction alone causes improvement without superior teacher assignment.
stress_test_results.original_evidence_holding: Smaller classes allow more individual instruction.
stress_test_results.attacked_condition: Random teacher assignment including novice educators.
stress_test_results.breaking_point_explanation: PASSED: Instruction quality modulates magnitude, but smaller class size retains positive signal independent of teacher tenure.

fragility.explanation_summary: The claim relies on valid primary-grade research, but breaks down severely when extrapolating a 35% causal STEM graduation gain across all demographics without longitudinal evidence past 8th grade.

verdict_justification: Primary grade benefits are verified (subclaim 1), but the claimed 35% high school STEM graduation boost and universal demographic uniformity are unsupported by available longitudinal data.
boundary_summary: Evidence boundary ends at Grade 8 standardized assessment scores for economically disadvantaged cohorts. Beyond Grade 8, the claim is speculative extrapolation.
killer_questions: What longitudinal study tracks STAR project participants through high school STEM major completion?
Does the 35% graduation increase hold when controlling for high school AP science course availability?
Why does the claim assert universal demographic application when Dynarski et al. prove heterogeneous outcomes?
missing_evidence_requirements: Longitudinal cohort tracking data linking K-3 class size to Grade 12 STEM diploma completion.
Comparative trial evaluating class-size impact in suburban vs Title I high schools.
Statistical mediation analysis controlling for high school teacher quality and tutoring access.
evidence_mutations: Source quote 'modest 4.2% algebra bump' mutated into '35% direct increase in STEM graduation rates'.
Source quote 'effects significant only for economically disadvantaged' mutated into 'across all socioeconomic demographics'.
